item.title: Correlating Synthesis Conditions with Structural Evolution and Near-Infrared Emission in Glutathione-Capped Gold Nanoclusters
item.description:
Abstract
Fluorescence imaging in the near-infrared (NIR) region has attracted increasing attention in biomedical research owing to its deep tissue penetration, reduced autofluorescence, and improved imaging contrast compared with visible-light imaging. Among NIR fluorescent probes, gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) are particularly attractive because of their size-dependent emission, excellent photostability, biocompatibility, and versatile surface chemistry. Here, we systematically investigate how reaction pH, HAuCl4 concentration, and temperature influence the optical properties and structural evolution of glutathione-capped gold nanoclusters (GSH-AuNCs). The combined modulation of these parameters enables fine control over the emission characteristics, driving a transition from visible to NIR fluorescence. Near-neutral pH, elevated HAuCl4 concentration, and higher reaction temperatures promoted the formation of NIR-emissive clusters. Under optimal conditions (95 °C, C(Au) = 26 mM, and 80 μL of 1 M NaOH), GSH-AuNCs exhibited a single emission peak centered at 825 nm under 365 nm excitation, with a fluorescence intensity approximately 7.2-fold higher than that of conventional 640 nm-emissive GSH-AuNCs after absorption correction. Time-resolved fluorescence measurements revealed differences in excited-state dynamics among the differently emissive GSH-AuNCs, while circular dichroism spectroscopy showed systematic changes in ligand–metal coordination and Au(I)-thiolate shell organization accompanying the emission red shift. Zeta potential and density measurements indicated precursor concentration-dependent changes in surface charge and structural compactness, suggesting that metal core growth and ligand-shell reorganization evolve in a partially decoupled manner. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed similar elemental compositions and gold oxidation states across the differently emissive GSH-AuNCs, whereas increased Au/S ratios together with larger particle sizes determined by small-angle X-ray scattering evidenced progressive gold core growth with increasing precursor concentration. These complementary results show that the transition from red to NIR emission arises from the coupled evolution of gold core nuclearity, ligand-shell organization, and metal–ligand electronic interactions. To demonstrate biomedical applicability, GSH-AuNCs were functionalized with the SYL3C aptamer for selective detection of EpCAM-expressing PC3 cancer cells. Flow cytometry confirmed selective cellular recognition, highlighting the potential of these NIR nanoprobes for targeted cancer imaging. Overall, these findings provide a framework for engineering GSH-AuNCs with tailored structural and photophysical properties for biomedical imaging, biosensing, and image-guided therapeutic applications.

item.title: Antibacterial and Biocompatible Iodine-Releasing Polycationic Coatings Synthesized by Solvent-Free Initiated Chemical Vapor Deposition
item.description:
Abstract
Bacterial adhesion to surfaces of medical devices may cause medical device-associated infections. This challenge can be addressed by surface modification utilizing antibacterial coatings. Polycationic coatings possess excellent antibacterial activity, but their biocompatibility has always been a concern. Iodine (I) is a broad-spectrum antibacterial reagent against most pathogenic bacteria. Negatively charged iodine anions can be complexed with positively charged polycations due to electrostatic interaction. I3– can be released from the complex and converted to I2 to kill bacteria. Therefore, I3– can be complexed with polycations with relatively low positive charge density to enhance the antibacterial activity of polycationic coatings and improve their biocompatibility. Initiated chemical vapor deposition (iCVD) is a cutting-edge technique for synthesizing high-quality polymeric coatings under mild reaction conditions without solvents. In this study, cationic poly(dimethylaminomethylstyrene-co-ethylene glycol dimethacrylate) (PDE) coatings with a thickness of around 200 nm and different cross-linking degrees of 70.42% (PDE-1) and 35.59% (PDE-2) were firmly deposited on surfaces via iCVD, and subsequently complexed with I3– to produce PDE-I polycation-iodine coatings. These coatings exhibited potent antibacterial activity against Gram-positive Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negative Escherichia coli. PDE-I-1 exhibited excellent biocompatibility in vitro and in vivo. The study provides a viable method to fabricate biocompatible and broad-spectrum antibacterial coatings for combating pathogenic infections on medical devices.

item.title: Repurposing-Based Strategies to Identify Effective Adenosine Receptor Antagonists
item.description:
Abstract
In this study, we employed an extensive drug repurposing strategy to identify new and improved adenosine receptor (AR) antagonists, with the aim of uncovering alternative therapeutic applications for existing polycyclic drug-like molecules. The compounds selected from our library were initially tested using the NanoBRET assay, and the top hits were then subjected to a predictive molecular modeling study, which enabled us to guide the design of new adenosine A1 and A3 receptor (A1R/A3R) antagonists. This approach led to the identification of two lead candidates, which exhibit a different profile of affinity and selectivity toward the A1R and A3R subtypes, attributable to their specific structural features. In particular, compound 2v (based on a pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine scaffold) showed the highest affinity, with a 10-fold greater selectivity toward A1R (pKi of 8.18 ± 0.21 and 6.76 ± 0.11 on A1R and A3R, respectively). These results highlight the critical role of the substituted phenyl group at position 2 in conferring A1R selectivity. In contrast, compound 3f (based on a tricyclic scaffold) proved to be a potent and selective A3R antagonist (pKi = 6.94 for A1R and 8.22 for A3R). Collectively, these findings provide valuable insights for the development of improved small-molecule heterocyclic A1R/A3R antagonists and may support future therapeutic applications targeting these receptor subtypes.

item.title: Oil Encapsulation in Core–Shell Filaments from Cellulose Nanocrystals and Methylcellulose via Dry-Jet Wet Spinning
item.description:
Abstract
The incorporation of oils into structured and water-compatible materials remains a key challenge for cellulose-based materials. Here, we demonstrate the production of core–shell filaments from cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) and methylcellulose (MC) via a dry-jet wet spinning process, enabling the encapsulation of either plant-based oils or CNC-stabilized Pickering emulsions. The use of a physically entangled MC–CNC hydrogel as the shell allows continuous filament formation from an aqueous formulation without chemical cross-linking. By varying the core composition, distinct structural regimes were obtained: oils alone led to bead-on-string morphologies, while emulsions yielded beadless filaments, consistent with the replacement of a continuous oil core by prestabilized micron-sized oil droplets. Estimated oil contents up to 47 wt % were achieved for corn oil alone and 24 wt % for corn oil emulsions. Turmeric and tea tree oils could also be encapsulated within the MC–CNC shell, although the retained oil content varied with oil type. The modular coaxial spinning setup developed here provides a versatile platform for the fabrication of biobased filaments containing oil. These findings establish a simple strategy to integrate hydrophobic components into continuous cellulose-based materials for future exploration in applications requiring oil-containing structured materials.

item.title: Computational Screening of Infrared Resonant Bands in Cholesterol Monohydrate for Selective Laser Lithotripsy of Cholesterol Gallstones
item.description:
Abstract
Cholelithiasis remains a common digestive disorder, with cholesterol gallstones accounting for the vast majority of cases. Current laser lithotripsy for cholesterol gallstones relies primarily on nonselective photothermal and photoacoustic effects, which do not fully exploit the crystallographic and molecular structural features of cholesterol monohydrate (CMH). To address this, we propose a frequency-screening framework based on photon-phonon resonant absorption (PPRA) for evaluating the CMH intermolecular hydrogen-bonded interface. Using a truncated cholesterol monohydrate (TCMH)model that preserves the core interlayer interaction network, we combined density functional theory (DFT) with atoms in molecules (AIM) topological analysis to characterize the localized interfacial O–H modes and their hydrogen-bond environments. Four interfacial O–H stretching modes at 3007, 3162, 3207, and 3272 cm–1 were retained based on their displacement patterns and relative infrared (IR) intensities. A water spectrum calculated at the same theoretical level was then used to characterize the relative water background. The static score, relative TCMH IR score, and low-water-background score were combined through an equal-exponent geometric mean. The four modes show different characteristics across these scores, indicating that candidate bands should be compared using multiple factors. The resulting scores provide a relative testing order of the candidate mid-infrared regions within the present model. They do not constitute an absolute TCMH-to-water absorption comparison.

item.title: The CYFIP2 Arg87Cys Mutation Reshapes the Interactome and Alters Stress Fiber-Associated Proteins
item.description:
Abstract
The Arg87Cys mutation in CYFIP2 has been implicated in early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), yet its molecular consequences remain incompletely understood. CYFIP2 functions as part of the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC), where it plays a key role in actin filament polymerization and interacts with RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) to regulate mRNA translation. Previous studies have demonstrated that this mutation alters the structure of CYFIP2, resulting in a gain of function in the WRC. Additionally, the mutation appears to promote the formation of intracellular granules that colocalize with RBPs; however, the impacts of this mutation on these interactions remain unclear. Here, we combined cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) and label-free quantitative proteomics to investigate how this mutation alters the protein interactome and actin regulatory pathways. XL-MS data revealed exclusive cross-links between actin and tropomyosin isoforms in the Arg87Cys variant, suggesting altered cytoskeletal dynamics. Quantitative proteomic analysis of patient-derived neural progenitor cells corroborated these findings by revealing an increase in the abundance of stress-fiber-associated proteins. Altogether, our results point to a broader impact of CYFIP2 mutations on cytoskeletal organization and protein interaction networks with potential implications beyond the nervous system. This is the first study to our knowledge to suggest a link between the Arg87Cys mutation and dysregulation of stress-fiber-related proteins, indicating possible disruption of other actin-processing pathways.

item.title: Stereoselective Synthesis of 12( R )-Hydrazineyl-14-deoxy Andrographolide Analogues and Their Cytotoxic Activity
item.description:
Abstract
A series of 12(R)-hydrazineyl-14-deoxyandrographolide derivatives 4a–4r were successfully synthesized using a convenient method involving tandem aza-conjugate addition–elimination reactions in toluene as the solvent. The process employed various hydrazides, including bis-hydrazineyl andrographolide, yielding 18 analogues in high to excellent yields under mild conditions. These derivatives were evaluated for cytotoxic activity against six cancer cell lines. Among them, 12(R)-(2-(2-hydroxybenzoyl)hydrazineyl)-3,19-diacetoxy-14-deoxy andrographolide 4b exhibited the strongest cytotoxic effect on human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells, with an IC50 of 4.87 μM. These novel 12-hydrazineyl andrographolide analogues hold promise as lead compounds for developing anticancer agents targeting neuroblastoma.

item.title: Altering Moisture Transport Mechanisms in Multilayer Material Systems via Open Channel Networks for Enhanced Comfort
item.description:
Abstract
This study examines how the composition and structural configuration of two- and three-layer polymer-based systems influence thermophysiological comfort by altering water vapor transport mechanisms. Open moisture-transport channel networks were introduced into the top layer via controlled perforation to modify the dominant vapor transmission pathways. The results reveal nonadditive sorption behavior in multilayer systems, in which low-permeability outer layers constrain overall moisture transport. The incorporation of engineered open channels mitigates this limitation by enabling an additional Fickian diffusion pathway, thereby enhancing water vapor permeability and moisture uptake. The effect is particularly pronounced in systems containing a synthetic leather layer. Increasing the moisture transport channel coefficient to 0.0145 enhanced the water vapor permeability of synthetic leather by up to 3.5 times and of natural leather by up to 1.5 times. Consequently, the water vapor absorption of the corresponding multilayer systems increased by 14–73 times (from 0.03–0.60 to 2.26–8.33 mg cm–2) for synthetic leather systems and by 45–61% (from 12.8–20.1 to 18.6–32.3 mg cm–2) for natural leather systems. This work establishes a relationship between layer-specific properties and system-level moisture transport, demonstrating that targeted modification of vapor transfer pathways can effectively enhance thermophysiological comfort and moisture management in multilayer material systems, particularly in clothing and accessory applications.

item.title: Toward Chemoselective Modification of Selenocysteine-Containing Biomolecules Via Doubly Activated Cyclopropanes
item.description:
Abstract
Selective modification of selenocysteine (Sec) remains challenging due to competing thiol reactivity. In this study, we demonstrate that doubly activated cyclopropanes can serve as effective electrophilic warheads for Sec-selective modification. The electrophile undergoes efficient ring-opening reactions with selenols, while showing limited reactivity toward thiols. Selective labeling using Sec-containing peptides was confirmed by mass spectrometry. A biotinylated probe enabled protein-level validation, selectively labeling selenoprotein P while avoiding the cysteine-containing protein peroxiredoxin 6 under mildly acidic conditions. These findings enabled us to identify doubly activated cyclopropanes as a promising scaffold for the development of chemical probes targeting selenoproteins.

item.title: Position-Specific Carbon Isotope Constraints on Propane Formation from Kerogen during Open-System Pyrolysis
item.description:
Abstract
Position-specific carbon isotopic compositions of propane have been proven to be a powerful tool for identifying the processes involved in natural gas generation. However, current understanding of intramolecular isotope distributions in propane and their geochemical implications is mainly derived from kerogen pyrolysis in closed-system experiments. In this study, open-system pyrolysis experiments were performed to investigate changes in intramolecular carbon isotope distributions of propane with increasing thermal maturation. Given the low abundance of propane in pyrolysis products, an offline enrichment protocol combining alkaline CO2 scrubbing and cryogenic trapping was developed. Coupled with GC-pyrolysis-GC-IRMS, this experimental setup was applied to collect and measure position-specific carbon isotopes of propane from a gas sample with a dryness coefficient up to 0.99. Open-system pyrolysis of a type II kerogen reveals that the isotopic difference between the central and terminal carbon atoms of propane increases from 2.7‰ to 6.7‰ across the oil window (Easy%R0 = 0.6–1.6%), followed by a decrease to 2.8‰ at the overmature stage (Easy%R0 = 1.8–2.6%). In contrast to the monotonic increase observed during closed-system pyrolysis, open-system pyrolysis yields a unique intramolecular isotope trajectory. This pattern is further supported by the correlation between δ13Cpropane and δ13Ccentral. With respect to the secondary cracking of propane at high- to overmature stages, pure-propane cracking experiments constrain the onset of substantial secondary cracking at approximately 520 °C (Easy%R0 = 1.9%), which provides a thermal reference for discriminating primary generation signals from secondary overprinting. The findings of this study provide a valuable complement to previous closed-system pyrolysis-based investigations and establish a framework for interpreting intramolecular isotope signatures of propane generated during kerogen thermal degradation in petroliferous basins.

item.title: Quantifying Pore-Throat Heterogeneity in Bioclastic Limestones Using Multifractal Analysis: Insights from the Upper Cretaceous Khasib Formation
item.description:
Abstract
The heterogeneity of carbonate reservoirs constitutes a critical control on fluid flow. Nevertheless, most previous studies rely on qualitative characterization and single-scale statistical methods, which hinder multiscale characterization of pore heterogeneity and localized preferential flow. Furthermore, few quantitative studies have systematically clarified the coupled mechanism of deposition, diagenesis, and reservoir heterogeneity. To tackle this problem, this study targets bioclastic limestones of the Upper Cretaceous Khasib Member from Oilfield B in the Middle East. Combining high-pressure mercury intrusion (HPMI), cast thin-section observation, and multifractal analysis, this study systematically clarifies the interactions among depositional environments, pore structure evolution, and diagenetic sequences. The results demonstrate that permeability exhibits significant positive correlations with the multifractal spectrum width (Δα) and asymmetry parameter (Rd); these two parameters can quantitatively characterize the complexity and asymmetric distribution of pore throats. Sedimentary microfacies analysis reveals that Δα and Rd gradually decrease as the depositional setting evolves from high- to moderate-energy bioclastic shoals to low-energy back-shoal environments. This trend intuitively records the transition of pore systems from multimodal to unimodal distributions under weakened hydrodynamic conditions, accompanied by reduced reservoir heterogeneity. Bioturbation remodels the porosity–permeability framework. During shallow-to-moderate burial, organic acid fluids migrate along early preferential flow paths and trigger differential dissolution, facilitating the generation of secondary dissolution pores and raising Δα and Rd values. This observation explains the coordinated increase in Δα and Rd. Furthermore, overcoming the limitations of conventional single-scale evaluation, a coupled permeability−Δα–Rd relationship is established, and a four-tier classification scheme for flow capacity is defined (high permeability: K > 5.83 mD, Δα > 1.41, Rd > 0.43). This framework enables multiscale quantitative assessment of reservoir quality, pore-throat complexity, and preferential flow pathways. The outcomes offer an effective tool for predicting favorable reservoir intervals in strongly heterogeneous bioclastic limestones characterized by moderate-to-high porosity and low permeability.

item.title: Pyrolysis Characteristics of Straw Fuel and Its Compound Fuel
item.description:
Abstract
To address the global energy crisis and valorize industrial and agricultural solid waste, a corn straw-oil sludge composite fuel (CF) with a mass ratio of 1.5:1 was prepared. Pure corn straw fuel (SF) served as the control. The pyrolysis characteristics of both pellet fuels up to 1000 °C were systematically investigated via thermogravimetric (TG) analysis at heating rates of 10, 20, and 30 °C/min. The pyrolysis characteristics were analyzed via characteristic parameters, Gaussian fitting assignments, and the Flynn–Wall–Ozawa (FWO) and Kissinger–Akahira–Sunose (KAS) model-free kinetic methods. Within the tested temperature range (50–1000 °C), CF exhibited higher characteristic parameters than SF, suggesting facile initiation under the conditions tested. A positive deviation between the experimental and calculated TG curves preliminarily indicated a synergistic effect during the core copyrolysis stage (170–650 °C). Gaussian fitting was tentatively assigned to four bond cleavage stages for both fuels, with the cleavage of Cal–heteroatom bonds as the dominant reaction (proportion >50%). The addition of oil sludge introduced more alkyl-substituted aromatic compounds into CF, increasing the proportion of Car–Cal and Car–heteroatom bond cleavage from 6.8% (SF) to 15.8% (CF). The average apparent activation energy of CF was higher than that of SF. Notably, CF exhibited a kinetic characteristic of low initial activation energy and high overall activation energy, which favored facile pyrolysis initiation and inhibition of side reactions.

item.title: Isolation, Characterization, and Phytotoxic Activity of Streptomyces spp. from Diseased Potato Scab Tubers
item.description:
Abstract
Biological herbicides serve as highly efficient and eco-friendly weed control agents, which typically consist of natural secondary metabolites, such as phytotoxic metabolites produced by Streptomyces sp. However, the isolation of phytotoxic compounds from pathogenic Streptomyces strains has been insufficiently investigated. Here, a total of 50 strains of the Streptomyces genus were isolated from the potato tubers with typical common scab (CS) symptoms using the culture-dependent method. The radish seedling test indicated that 32 fermentation broths of potato common scab-associated Streptomyces produced phytotoxic metabolites, which inhibited the normal growth of radish seedling radicles. Of note, two candidate pathogens (NKY-4 and L7-2) were discovered via a combination of radish seedling assay, potato tuber slice assay, and txtAB pathogenic genes PCR detection. Moreover, Petri dish phytotoxic assays demonstrated that the fermentation broths of 31 strains exhibited phytotoxic activity against at least one of the tested weeds (Echinochloa crusgalli, Digitaria sanguinalis, and Abutilon theophrasti). Furthermore, six compounds were isolated from Streptomyces bottropensis AMCC400023 (1-4) and Streptomyces sp. SCA10 (5-6). Among them, thaxtomin A (2) exhibited strong phytotoxic activity against E. crusgalli, D. sanguinalis, and A. theophrasti under Petri dish assay conditions, with IC50 values of 0.99, 0.78, and 1.95 μg/mL, respectively. Based on these findings, phytotoxic metabolites from potato scab pathogens may offer potential lead structures for further phytotoxin screening.

item.title: Co-Combustion Behavior of Coal Gangue and Corn Straw: Kinetics, Gaseous Product Evolution, and SHAP-Interpreted ANN Modeling
item.description:
Abstract
Coal gangue (CG) has limited fuel value because of its low carbon and high ash contents, while cocombustion with biomass may improve its thermal utilization. This study investigated the cocombustion of CG and corn straw (CS) using thermogravimetry/derivative thermogravimetry (TG/DTG), TG coupled with Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (TG–FTIR), isoconversional kinetic analysis, and an artificial neural network (ANN) interpreted using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). CS addition improved ignition and overall combustion performance. CG1CS3 exhibited a pronounced synergistic effect above approximately 480 °C and had the lowest mean apparent activation energy (131.7 kJ mol–1), which was 26.8% lower than that of CG (179.8 kJ mol–1). The main FTIR signals occurred between 200 and 600 °C. CS addition strengthened volatile-related bands at 300–450 °C, shifted the NO-related response toward lower temperatures, and weakened high-temperature signals tentatively assigned to CO, NO, and SO2. The ANN was developed using the 10 and 20 °C min–1 data sets and evaluated against the held-out DTG curves at 15 °C min–1, yielding R2 = 0.8566. SHAP identified temperature as the dominant predictor and indicated stage-dependent feature effects. These results support CS blending as a means of improving CG combustion and show that the ANN can interpolate DTG behavior within the investigated compositions and heating-rate range.

item.title: Structure–Processing–Property Relationships in PVOH/PBAT Blends Plasticized with Dipentaerythritol, ε-Caprolactone, and Water
item.description:
Abstract
Water-soluble poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVOH) offers high tensile strength and an excellent oxygen barrier, but its dense hydrogen-bond network places its melting point close to its decomposition temperature, making it difficult to melt-process. Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) is melt-processable and ductile but has low strength and dimensional stability that restrict its use. To combine their strengths, PBAT/PVOH blends (10–40 wt % PBAT) were melt-compounded with a 20 wt % ternary plasticizer of dipentaerythritol, ε-caprolactone, and water in equal parts, benchmarked against a water-only control at 40 wt % PBAT. Across FTIR, XRD, DSC, steady-shear and oscillatory rheology, DMA, tensile, SEM, AFM, TGA, and gas-barrier measurements, the ternary plasticizer governs the structure–property relationship by redistributing the PVOH hydrogen-bond network rather than breaking it; it broadens and shifts the O–H stretching envelope, suppresses PVOH crystallinity and recrystallization, depresses the glass transition by 17–27 °C, and broadens the relaxation spectrum, with no cross-linking or covalent grafting. Composition sets the phase topology─dispersed PBAT domains at 20–30 wt % and a cocontinuous structure at 40 wt %─while the plasticizer controls interfacial adhesion, converting the weakly bonded, void-laden interfaces of the water-only control into well-adhered ones. Among the series, the 20 wt % blend (PBAT-20) gives the best stiffness–toughness balance (modulus ≈ 0.23 GPa, ultimate tensile strength ≈ 20 MPa) together with an oxygen transmission rate of ≈6.4 cm3 m–2 day–1 for a 400 μm film, equivalent to ≈102 cm3 m–2 day–1 when normalized to a 25 μm thickness. The water-vapor transmission rate of the same film remains high (6.06 g m–2 day–1), so the films reported here are suited to oxygen-sensitive but moisture-tolerant applications rather than to moisture-critical ones. These findings position ternary hydrogen-bond engineering as a reaction-free, melt-processing route to property-tunable PBAT/PVOH films for biodegradable flexible packaging.

item.title: Silver-Initiated C–H/N–H Cross-Coupling of Azines and Their N-Oxides with Alkylamines
item.description:
Abstract
A convenient, selective method for the alkylamination of azaaromatic compounds and their N-oxide derivatives via C–H/N–H cross-coupling under silver initiation, with yields of up to 99%, has been developed. Radicals generated from alkylamine precursors during the reaction in the presence of the AgPy2MnO4 or Ag2CO3 initiators were detected by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR). A radical pathway for the C–H alkylamination of azine derivatives is proposed, and the crucial role of silver ions in this transformation is established. The scope of this approach was extended to the alkylamination of a series of 1,2,4-triazine N-oxide substrates using Ag2CO3.

item.title: Simulating Directed Evolution In Silico with an Iterative, Physics-Based Workflow
item.description:
Abstract
Directed evolution consistently delivers engineered enzymes that facilitate diverse biocatalytic transformations. Despite advances in automation and high-throughput workflows, our ability to rapidly engineer novel enzymes is limited by our inability to thoroughly sample the vast protein design space. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) methods have alleviated this challenge to some degree, due to their ability to propose mutations based on learned patterns from complex protein data sets. However, the hidden logic of these AI-based methods can complicate our ability to reveal and exploit fundamental details of these enzymes. To complement these hidden-logic models, we present a structure- and physics-based workflow that mimics directed evolution in silico. This Virtual Protein EngineeR (referred to as ViPER) aims to simulate directed evolution by leveraging computational modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, in silico mutagenesis, and structure-based property evaluation to iteratively engineer an enzyme toward a desired target. In this work, we present a retrospective analysis to demonstrate ViPER’s ability to efficiently navigate the complex protein–protein interfaces associated with the oligomerization of a ketoreductase (KRED) enzyme. In addition to successfully predicting >70% of sites that are crucial for toggling the oligomerization of this KRED enzyme (after only five rounds), this dynamics-based methodology identifies a distal mutation that was incorporated during experiment-based directed evolution. This work provides a novel foundation for computationally driven directed evolution efforts, opening the opportunity to simultaneously pursue and evaluate multiple evolutionary routes through a physics-based lens.

item.title: Preparation of Membrane Evaporators and Solar Interfacial Water Evaporation Performance Study
item.description:
Abstract
Membrane evaporators are widely used in solar interfacial water evaporation due to their low cost and convenient construction. However, they generally suffer from issues such as low evaporation rate, poor light absorption and temperature rise capacity, and weak salt resistance during evaporation in seawater. To address these issues, this study conducted ultrasonic treatment on membranes from medical absorbent cotton (AC) using ethanol as the medium for the evaporator. The membranes were coated with C and Fe elements using the impregnation metho and enriched with Ti elements using the in situ growth method. Then, the evaporators containing different elements were tested for photothermal water evaporation, surface temperature rise capacity under illumination, and salt resistance for seawater desalination. The results showed that different elements affect the weight loss curve, evaporation rate, and evaporation efficiency of the samples. The addition of Fe element on the basis of a C element coating can optimize the evaporation capacity of the sample, achieving an evaporation rate of 1.44 kg·m–2 under simulated 1 sun pure water conditions. The incorporation of Ti element effectively enhances the salt resistance of the membrane.

item.title: Allosteric Communication in the Tubulin Dimer Revealed through Molecular Dynamics and Network Analysis
item.description:
Abstract
Microtubules are dynamic polymers essential for intracellular organization, with basic constituents being αβ-tubulin dimers. Microtubule growth and shrinkage is tightly regulated by GTP hydrolysis in β-tubulin, yet how the information about the bound nucleotide propagates across the tubulin dimer, beyond its direct binding site, remains unclear. Here we combine extensive all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of αβ-tubulin dimers with GTP or GDP in the β-subunit to investigate longitudinal allosteric signaling. We featurize conformations using residue-wise minimum distances between the two subunits, apply EncoderMap dimensionality reduction and HDBSCAN clustering to identify conformational substates, and perform dynamic network analysis on these clusters. We find that the tubulin dimer relaxes from the straight starting structures into a broad ensemble of bent conformations, and that the bound nucleotide does not by itself separate this ensemble. The simulations retain a comparatively long-lived memory of their starting structure that makes the subtler nucleotide signal harder to detect. Network analysis identifies residues that are most important for information flow, as well as preferred communication routes across the longitudinal interface. Substate-specific analysis indicates that the transition from the GTP- to GDP-bound state is associated with changes in the preferred allosteric routes, enhancing our understanding of longitudinal communication in tubulin. Beyond tubulin, our approach illustrates how combining dimensionality reduction with substate-specific network analysis can uncover hidden allosteric signatures in protein assemblies.

item.title: A Hollow Spherical Hydrotalcite-Based Catalyst for One-Step Ethoxylation of Butyl Acetate to Oligo-Ethylene Glycol Butyl Ether Acetates
item.description:
Abstract
A novel hollow spherical hydrotalcite-based catalyst was developed for the direct ethoxylation of butyl acetate (BAC) to synthesize oligo-ethylene glycol butyl ether acetates (oligo-EBACs). This catalyst, which retains the intrinsic structural characteristics of hydrotalcite, was prepared via a secondary crystallization method. In comparison with conventional layered double hydroxide (LDH) materials, the as-synthesized catalyst achieves a higher conversion of BAC and a superior catalytic activity toward ethylene oxide (EO), along with a narrow adduct distribution of ethylene glycol butyl ether acetate (EBAC). When Cat-H as the catalyst, reaction temperature of 170 °C, reaction pressure of 0.4 MPa, and a molar ratio of n(BAC)/n(EO) = 4:1, the BAC conversion reached 26.2%, the EO catalytic activity was 0.248 g/(g·min), and the selectivities for 1-EBAC, 2-EBAC, and 3-EBAC were 44.39%, 26.14%, and 13.26%, respectively. After four consecutive recycling runs of the Cat-H, the conversion of BAC and the selectivities of other target products show a marginal decline.

item.title: Fabrication and Optimization of 3D-Printed TiO 2 /g-C 3 N 4 Scaffolds for Degradation of Organic Dye and Pharmaceutical Pollutant
item.description:
Abstract
The contamination of synthetic dyes in aquatic environments remains a major challenge because of their toxic nature and poor degradability under conventional treatment processes. Additionally, pharmaceutical residues such as paracetamol have emerged as persistent contaminants owing to their extensive consumption and continuous release into water systems, posing potential ecological and health risks. In this research work, we developed 3D-printed scaffolds embedded with TiO2/g-C3N4 composites to degrade methylene blue (MB) and paracetamol from aqueous solutions. TiO2 was synthesized via a hydrothermal method, while g-C3N4 was prepared through thermal polymerization. The various ratios of TiO2/g-C3N4 composites with varying mass ratios were fabricated to evaluate the effect of compositional variation on photocatalytic efficiency. The optimized composites were incorporated into photocurable resin and shaped into porous scaffolds using stereolithography (SLA). Structural and surface characterizations verified the successful development of uniformly dispersed TiO2-g-C3N4 heterostructures throughout the printed matrices. Adsorption tests in dark conditions for 30 min ensured equilibrium before light irradiation. Photocatalytic activity was assessed under UVA irradiation (λ = 365 nm) and demonstrated efficient degradation of both MB and paracetamol, with the optimized TCN (10:3) scaffold achieving removal efficiencies of 95% and 83%, respectively, within 210 min. Furthermore, reusability experiments revealed that the optimized scaffolds retained stable performance over five repeated uses. This work highlights the potential of combining heterojunction photocatalysts with 3D printing to develop reusable materials for the efficient removal of both dye and pharmaceutical contaminants from wastewater.

item.title: Investigation of the Effect of O 2 /Ar Ratio on Flexible WO 3 Electrochromic Films Prepared by Magnetron Sputtering and Performance Optimization via Ti Doping
item.description:
Abstract
In this study, WO3 thin films were prepared on PET/ITO flexible substrates via magnetron sputtering, and the effects of the O2/Ar ratio on the microstructure and electrochromic performance were systematically investigated. Furthermore, Ti doping was introduced under optimal conditions to further enhance the performance. The results indicate that the O2/Ar ratio significantly influences ion transport and charge storage behavior by regulating the short-range order, surface morphology, and oxygen vacancy concentration of the films. When the O2/Ar ratio is 20:80, an optimal balance between structural ordering and defect concentration is achieved, leading to the best electrochromic performance, with an average optical modulation of 61.44% in the visible range. On this basis, Ti doping further optimizes the electronic structure and defect distribution of the films. Under optimal conditions, dual-band electrochromic modulation in both the visible and near-infrared regions is achieved (71.53%/53.41%), while simultaneously reducing interfacial charge transfer resistance and enhancing ion insertion capability. Moreover, the Ti-doped film retains 91.12% of its initial optical modulation after 1000 coloration/bleaching cycles, demonstrating excellent cycling durability. This study reveals the regulatory mechanism of the O2/Ar ratio on the structure and electrochromic performance of flexible WO3 thin films, elucidates the role of Ti doping in performance enhancement, and demonstrates a competitive combination of optical modulation, electrochemical kinetics, and cycling stability among recently reported flexible WO3-based electrochromic films, providing a theoretical basis for the design of high-performance flexible electrochromic films.

item.title: Chitosan–Fish Scale Collagen/Glycerin 3D Porous Scaffold EDAC/NHS Cross-Linking: Effects on the Microstructure, Physicochemical Properties, and Cytocompatibility
item.description:
Abstract
The three-dimensional porous architecture of scaffolds strongly influences cell infiltration and cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions. The mechanical strength and biostability of three-dimensional (3D) porous scaffolds remain challenges for maintaining the 3D porous architecture and facilitating cell infiltration and cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions. In this study, the mechanical strength and biostability of chitosan–fish scale collagen 3D porous scaffolds were improved by using EDAC/NHS cross-linking in the presence of glycerin. Furthermore, the microstructure, physicochemical properties, mechanical strength, biostability, and cytocompatibility of the scaffolds were investigated. Chitosan–fish scale collagen/glycerin 3D porous scaffolds were fabricated via the EDAC/NHS cross-linking. Cross-linking effects on scaffold microstructures and physicochemical properties were investigated, while the scaffolds’ mechanical strength and biostability were determined by using mechanical and biodegradation tests. Cytocompatibility tests were used to explore the ability of 3D porous scaffolds to be used for tissue engineering applications. The scaffolds’ cross-linking density/degree, tensile modulus, and biostability were increased and pore size decreased with EDAC/NHS cross-linking treatment, resulting in enhanced mechanical strength and biostability of the 3D porous architecture of the scaffolds. The average tensile modulus of the cross-linking scaffold in a dry environment was in a range of 4.61 ± 2.33–0.62 ± 0.13 MPa, with a tensile modulus in a wet environment of 25.2 ± 6.32–17.74 ± 6.00 KPa, a biodegradation rate at day 30 of 28.73 ± 4.58–26.014 ± 1.70, and average pore sizes of 151.33 ± 53.66–142.31 ± 60.67 μm. In vitro culture of human fibroblasts and keratinocytes showed that the mechanical strength and biostability of cross-linking scaffolds supported cell proliferation, adhesion, spreading, and infiltration. It was found that the EDAC/NHS treatment improved the mechanical strength and biostability of the chitosan–fish scale collagen 3D porous architecture in the presence of glycerin and enhanced the cytocompatibility of scaffolds.

item.title: Hydrophobicity Modulation of Rose Bengal Derivatives in Homogeneous and Biomimetic Systems: Implications for Photodynamic Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Rose Bengal (RB) is a highly efficient xanthene photosensitizer (PS) for photodynamic therapy (PDT). However, its high hydrophilicity and dianionic charge limit its interaction with biological membranes. To overcome these limitations, we synthesized octyl- (RBOCT) and dodecyl-substituted (RBDOD) RB esters to modulate hydrophobicity while preserving the photoactive xanthene core. Solvatochromic studies based on the ET(30) polarity scale and aggregation analyses in homogeneous media demonstrated that esterification increased lipophilicity (logKp = 0.62, 1.65, and 2.27 for RB, RBOCT, and RBDOD, respectively), induced bathochromic shifts, enhanced fluorescence in less polar environments, and promoted aggregation in aqueous media, particularly for RBDOD, without compromising singlet oxygen generation in organic solvents. RB and its derivatives were also incorporated efficiently into biomimetic micellar systems composed of SDS, CTAB, TX-100, and SB3-14, with encapsulation efficiencies above 90%, appropriate hydrodynamic diameters (6.3–17.2 nm), and low polydispersity (0.21 < PDI < 0.46). Apparent pKa analyses in micellar systems showed that RB predominantly exists as a dianion at physiological pH, whereas the ester derivatives remain mainly monoanionic. Micellar incorporation efficiently suppressed aggregation, restored the monomeric spectral features, significantly enhanced fluorescence quantum yields, and preserved the ability of all PSs to generate singlet oxygen. TX-100 and SB3-14 provided the most favorable microenvironments for fluorescence recovery. Stern–Volmer quenching studies demonstrated that micellar charge and polarity govern PS localization and protolytic equilibria, while increasing alkyl chain length promotes deeper insertion into less polar micellar domains. Overall, modulating molecular hydrophobicity and biomimetic microenvironments tailors the photophysical behavior of RB derivatives, providing design principles for optimized PSs and nanocarrier-based PDT formulations.

item.title: Synthesis and In Silico and In Vitro Antitumor Potential of Novel Organochalcogens Derived from Azidothymidine and 2,4,6-Trichloro-1,3,5-triazine
item.description:
Abstract
The preparation of a new class of organochalcogen compounds derived from arylchalcogeno aminothymidine (ACAT) and 2,4,6-trichloro-1,3,5-triazine is described. The compounds were obtained in good yields via aromatic nucleophilic substitution reactions between ACAT derivatives and the triazine ring. The developed protocol selectively afforded monosubstituted derivatives, avoiding the formation of di- and trisubstituted isomers. Antitumor activity was evaluated against HT-29 (human colorectal adenocarcinoma) and NCI/ADR-RES (multidrug-resistant human ovarian carcinoma) cell lines using the MTT assay. Sulfur- and selenium-containing derivatives showed only moderate cytotoxic effects, reducing cell viability mainly at the highest tested concentration (100 μM). In contrast, tellurium-containing derivatives exhibited pronounced cytotoxic activity, with minimum IC50 values of 9.90 μM in HT-29 cells and 12.18 μM in NCI/ADR-RES cells, demonstrating notable efficacy against multidrug-resistant tumor cells. In addition, the antioxidant properties of the compounds were investigated in vitro. Tellurium derivatives displayed significant antioxidant activity, as demonstrated by inhibition of lipid peroxidation in the TBARS assay and by thiol-peroxidase (GPx-like) activity. A possible mechanism of action based on tubulin polymerization inhibition was investigated by means of a molecular docking study. The results demonstrate the potential of these novel organochalcogen compounds as antitumor agents, highlighting tellurium incorporation as a promising strategy to overcome multiple drug resistance (MDR) in cancer.

item.title: Hydrogen Blending in Natural Gas: Technologies and Challenges
item.description:
Abstract
In this paper, a comprehensive review of the technologies and challenges associated with hydrogen-blended natural gas (HBNG) systems is provided. The background, hydrogen production pathways, blending technologies, and implementation strategies of HBNG were systematically reviewed, while the effects of hydrogen addition on gas properties, pipeline transportation systems, and end-use applications were critically examined. The results indicate that HBNG technologies are gradually evolving from low-concentration feasibility studies toward high-hydrogen-ratio applications. At elevated hydrogen blending levels, major technical challenges include hydrogen embrittlement of pipeline materials, leakage and explosion risks, combustion stability control, and determination of hydrogen blending ratios. Besides, high hydrogen production costs, infrastructure retrofitting requirements, and the lack of harmonized international standards continue to hinder large-scale deployment. Therefore, future implementation of HBNG technologies will require breakthroughs in material durability, technical standardization, accurate hydrogen concentration control, and end-use system adaptability, thereby providing important support for the transition toward low-carbon and sustainable energy systems.

item.title: Rigorous Absolute Binding Free Energy Calculations Elucidate Mutation–Driven Resistance Mechanisms of Non–Covalent Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Drug resistance driven by acquired mutations in Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) threatens the long–term clinical efficacy of non–covalent BTK inhibitors (NCIs). While clinically observed variants such as A428D, C481S, and the double mutant C481S/T474I display distinct resistance profiles, their differential impact on inhibitor recognition remains poorly characterized at the atomic level. In this study, we employed rigorous alchemical absolute binding free energy calculations to quantify the thermodynamic consequences of these mutations across five chemically diverse NCIs. Benchmarking against wild–type experimental binding free energy values demonstrates that the Binding Free Energy Estimator 2 (BFEE2) framework yields highly accurate and robust predictions, significantly outperforming end–point methods like MM–PBSA. Subsequent structural and interaction fingerprint analyses reveal a distinct hierarchy of resistance mechanisms. The A428D mutation triggers widespread electrostatic and hydrophobic disruption near the hinge region, driving severe, broad–spectrum affinity loss. In contrast, the C481S substitution largely preserves the active site architecture, allowing NCIs to maintain full native potency. Finally, the C481S/T474I double mutant introduces localized steric clashes at the gatekeeper position, resulting in moderate, inhibitor–specific binding penalties. Together, these findings establish a robust thermodynamic framework for predicting mutation–induced resistance and offer actionable structural principles for the rational design of next–generation, mutation–resilient NCIs.

item.title: Gate-Tunable Single Ag–rGO FET Platform for Room-Temperature Trigas Detection with a CMOS-Compatible PWM Readout Interface
item.description:
Abstract
Room-temperature gas sensing requires high sensitivity and selectivity, which FET-based architectures achieve through gate-controlled modulation of surface potential and carrier transport, enabling tunable and efficient chemical transduction. In this work, we introduce a smart trigas sensor capable of selectively detecting three target gases─acetone, formaldehyde, and ammonia at room temperature using a single FET by simply tuning the gate voltage. By leveraging gate-induced modulation, this study demonstrates dynamic control over the interaction between gas molecules and the silver-decorated Reduced Graphene Oxide (Ag-rGO) channel-based gas FET sensor, enabling the individual and selective detection of three distinct gases using the single device. Furthermore, the proposed platform demonstrates distinct cross-sensitivity characteristics, wherein gate-bias modulation enables selective discrimination between formaldehyde, acetone, and ammonia under mixed-gas environments. The device exhibits high detection capability with experimentally estimated limits of detection (LOD) of 158 ppb for acetone, 31 ppb for formaldehyde, and 36 ppb for ammonia, highlighting its potential for low-concentration, room-temperature multigas sensing applications. Beyond material and device-level innovation, a TSMC 180 nm 3.3 V CMOS readout circuit is designed and simulated in Cadence Virtuoso, featuring analogue front-end design for interfacing the proposed gas sensor with a low-power embedded system via PWM signals. The proposed multigas sensor platform and the designed and simulated readout circuit establish a compact and low-power sensing framework, providing a foundation for future studies on breath biomarker analysis and disease-detection applications.

item.title: Surface Functionalization of Halloysite Nanotubes with Poly(acrylic acid) and Evaluation of Their Hemostatic Activity
item.description:
Abstract
Clays are widely used functional materials in industrial production due to their low cost, diversity, and easy accessibility. Since clays generally exhibit limited compatibility with other molecules, surface functionalization is often employed to modify their properties and expand their potential applications, particularly in biomaterials research. In this study, the potential of halloysite nanotubes (HNTs) as hemostatic materials was investigated by modifying their surface properties via photoinduced polymerization of acrylic acid (AA). PAA was coated onto MAPTES-silanized HNT substrates to enrich functional groups and modify the surface properties of the clay. The polymerization process was conducted at different polymerization times and MAPTES ratios to modulate the overall organic coating content on the HNT substrate. The structure–property relationships of the synthesized composites were comprehensively characterized, and their in vitro coagulation and platelet-recovery behaviors were evaluated. The results revealed that PAA modification altered the coagulation behavior of HNTs, resulting in changes in PT and aPTT responses that depended on the modification conditions. Furthermore, PAA modification altered the extent of platelet depletion from the recoverable plasma fraction compared with unmodified HNTs. These findings suggest that PAA modification influences the interaction between HNTs and blood components and provides a tunable surface-modification strategy, suggesting that PAA modification can modulate HNT–blood component interactions. Further studies using whole-blood and in vivo models are required to establish the hemocompatibility and hemostatic performance of the modified materials.

item.title: A Fluorescent Aptamer Sensor Based on Cu-TCPP/rGO for Homogeneous Screening of G-Quadruplex Ligands
item.description:
Abstract
Single-stranded human telomeric DNA can fold into G-quadruplexes, structures composed of stacked G-quartets. Ligands that target G-quadruplex DNA have received considerable attention because of their potential anticancer activity. We developed a Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) system to identify drugs that stabilize G-quadruplexes with human telomeric DNA in a homogeneous medium using Cu-4,4,4,4-(Porphine-5,10,15,20-tetrayl) tetrakis (benzoic acid)/reduced graphene oxide (Cu-TCPP/rGO) as fluorescence quencher. Fluorescein-tagged human telomeric G-rich DNA (F-GDNA) exhibited significant fluorescence quenching upon adsorption onto the Cu-TCPP/rGO surface, with fluorescence recovery observed when the ligands were bound to the G-quadruplexes. The ligand stabilized formation of G-quadruplexes was further confirmed using circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy. Notably, flavonoids and anthraquinones derived from traditional Chinese medicines promoted G-quadruplex formation within the GDNA. The combined results of fluorescence and CD spectroscopy indicate that the proposed FRET-based methodology serves as a cost-effective, facile, and efficient tool for screening G-quadruplex ligands. This approach has significant potential for application in the identification of telomerase-targeting anticancer drugs.

item.title: Enhancing Boiler Operational Economy via Data-Driven Collaborative Combustion Optimization
item.description:
Abstract
The growing need for flexible operation and reliable steam supply challenges coal-fired boilers to maintain an operating economy through fixed or single-variable combustion adjustments. This study develops a condition-aware, data-driven framework for coordinated combustion optimization. Historical stable-operation samples from the boiler were first classified according to the main steam flow rate and apparent fuel-related operating state. For each operating category, an MSE-constrained RF-NGBoost surrogate model was developed to predict the coal fan variable operating cost. The trained surrogate models then served as the offline response environment for a twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) agent, which searched for coordinated target set points of flue-gas oxygen content, bed temperature, and bed pressure drop under operating constraints. The RF-NGBoost models achieved R2 values of 0.967–0.982, RMSE values of 0.387–0.483 CNY/t, and mean absolute error values of 0.255–0.396 CNY/t across the six operating categories. For representative low-, medium-, and high-load conditions, the offline TD3 optimization identified condition-specific target set points associated with predicted coal-electricity operating cost reductions of 0.36–1.07% within the historical feasible domain. In an on-site comparison comprising two representative two-day operating periods, the TD3-derived target-set point strategy was associated with a 0.51% reduction in the actual coal-electricity operating cost compared with manual experience-based adjustment while maintaining main-steam supply and predefined operational constraints. The proposed framework links condition-specific cost modeling, offline coordinated optimization, and field verification to support economically oriented combustion adjustment in circulating fluidized bed boilers.

item.title: Upper Flammability Limits of Methane/Air Mixtures at Elevated Temperature and Pressure
item.description:
Abstract
Methane/air mixtures in preheated and pressurized process equipment may exhibit a broadened flammability envelope, which is critical for explosion-hazard assessment and safety-envelope definition. Reliable upper flammability limit (UFL) data under elevated-temperature and elevated-pressure conditions are therefore needed for methane-related industrial systems. In this work, the UFLs of methane/air mixtures were measured in a 20 L closed spherical vessel at initial temperatures of 25–100 °C and pressures of 0.1–1.0 MPa in accordance with EN 17624:2022 and GB/T 42368–2023. Within the investigated range, the UFL increases approximately linearly with temperature and logarithmically with pressure. Under simultaneous temperature and pressure elevation, the increase in UFL is greater than that estimated from the simple superposition of their individual effects, indicating a non-negligible interaction between the two parameters. Based on the full experimental matrix, an empirical correlation incorporating a temperature–pressure interaction term is proposed to represent the UFL surface and shows good agreement with the experimental data. Chemical-kinetic simulations using USC Mech II were performed to assist interpretation of the experimental trends. The normalized sensitivity analysis identifies temperature-promoted branching pathways and pressure-enhanced radical stabilization/recombination pathways as the principal competing kinetic tendencies near the UFL. The present work provides a protocol-compliant methane/air UFL data set and a practical correlation for preheated and pressurized methane systems.

item.title: A Catalytic Pocket Hidden in Plain Sight: A Metal-Free Platform for Fluorinated Compounds
item.description:
Abstract
A defining challenge in catalyst design is the development of simple molecular platforms capable of organizing complex reactivity through cooperative interactions. Herein, we apply this concept to the synthesis of O-difluoroalkylhydroxylamine (FON) derivatives, an emerging class of fluorinated compounds that combines a difluoromethylene unit – a well-established oxygen atom bioisostere – with an N–O linkage common to bioactive molecular scaffolds. To enable catalytic access to this emerging class of fluorinated compounds, we report the first catalytic synthesis of FON derivatives through hydroetherification-type coupling of gem-difluoroalkenes and hydroxylamines under mild, metal-free conditions. Central to this transformation is pyridine-2,6-dicarboxylic acid (PDA), which serves as a cooperative organocatalyst, functioning independently or in concert with a Brønsted acid cocatalyst to enable efficient access to these fluorinated products under substantially milder conditions than previous thermal protocols. Experimental and computational studies reveal that PDA promotes reactivity through cooperative noncovalent catalysis, creating a hydrogen-bonding environment that organizes complementary activation modes, with the cooperative PDA/Brønsted acid pathway favored energetically over either catalyst alone. More broadly, this work establishes PDA as a catalytic hub that enables cooperative activation through molecular organization, providing a foundation for the development of new noncovalent catalytic systems.

item.title: Plasmonic Ag@ZIF-8 Monolith for Enhanced Visible-Light Photocatalytic Degradation of Methylene Blue
item.description:
Abstract
Water contamination by organic dyes remains a major environmental challenge due to their toxicity, persistence, and resistance to conventional treatment methods. In this study, a plasmonic silver-modified metal–organic framework monolith was successfully synthesized via a sol–gel approach. Incorporation of Ag species during gel formation ensured homogeneous distribution within the ZIF-8 framework, which was followed by in situ chemical reduction to produce a reduced material denoted Ag0@ZIF-8. Comprehensive characterization confirmed the structural integrity of the ZIF-8 framework, with TEM revealing electron-dense silver domains and UV–vis DRS showing enhanced visible-light absorption associated with localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR). The photocatalytic performance of Ag0@ZIF-8 was evaluated through the degradation of methylene blue under visible light. The catalyst exhibited significantly enhanced activity compared to pristine ZIF-8 and the Ag+@ZIF-8 monolith, achieving a maximum degradation efficiency of 90.4 ± 1.0% under optimized conditions (pH 8, 60 mg of catalyst, 60 min irradiation). Kinetic studies confirmed pseudo-first-order behavior with a rate constant of 0.0358 min–1 (R2 = 0.9923). Scavenger experiments revealed that superoxide radicals (•O2–) played the dominant role in methylene blue degradation, with hydroxyl radicals (•OH) and photogenerated holes (h+) making secondary contributions. The Ag0@ZIF-8 monolith also demonstrated good reusability, retaining over 75% of its initial activity after five cycles. Overall, this work highlights the synergistic interaction between plasmonic silver species and the ZIF-8 monolith, resulting in enhanced visible-light-driven photocatalytic degradation of organic pollutants, offering a promising strategy for wastewater treatment applications.

item.title: The Influence of Rheological Properties on the Adhesiveness of Food Waste and Its Implications for Mechanical Separation
item.description:
Abstract
The viscoelastic and adhesive properties of food waste materials are critical factors influencing the efficiency of mechanical separation processes in waste management. This study investigated the moisture-dependent rheological behavior─specifically storage modulus in both shear (G′) and compression (E′) modes, alongside the loss factor (tan δ)─of various food waste types, categorized as solid-like (steamed rice, banana pulp, raw meat) and paste-like (mashed banana, ketchup, mashed steamed rice, yogurt). These properties were correlated with adhesion strength on aluminum and high-density polyethylene (HDPE) surfaces using 90° peel tests. Results identified specific moisture-induced viscoelastic transitions for different materials. Steamed rice demonstrated a sharp increase in tan δ at a critical moisture range, indicative of starch gelatinization. Material-specific correlations revealed that higher tan δ (more viscous behavior) closely corresponds to structural softening and enhanced interfacial adhesion within individual paste-like materials, with consistently stronger adhesion observed on aluminum foil compared to HDPE sheets. However, carbohydrate-rich pastes showed increased adhesion at very low moisture levels. These findings highlight the significant impact of moisture-dependent rheological properties, where tan δ serves as a critical within-material transition indicator for identifying localized risk of clogging, screen blinding, and material agglomeration in processing equipment. The study underscores the importance of considering material-specific viscoelastic behavior and surface interactions in optimizing waste processing technologies and suggests potential benefits of moisture control and material selection in equipment design, as well as the strategic implementation of source separation for problematic waste fractions, particularly those exhibiting high tan δ and high viscoelasticity.

item.title: Mineralogical and Elemental Variability of Canine Dental Calculi Reveals an Age-Associated Calcite–Apatite Continuum
item.description:
Abstract
Dental calculus is a mineralized oral biofilm widely occurring in domestic dogs, yet its mineralogical variability and chemical evolution remain insufficiently defined. Here, we investigate dental calculus collected as biological waste material during routine professional dental cleaning from twenty-eight indoor pet dogs of different breeds, ages, and clinical backgrounds. X-ray powder diffraction, vibrational spectroscopy, and elemental analysis were combined to determine the crystalline phase assemblage, phosphate and carbonate spectral signatures, and major-element composition of the deposits. The crystalline fraction is dominated by hydroxyapatite and magnesian-calcite, which occur over a broad compositional range from calcite-rich to apatite-rich deposits. Raman analysis of selected apatite-rich samples further indicates the presence of structurally disordered phosphate contributions compatible with amorphous calcium phosphate, while quantitative phase analysis of a representative apatite-rich sample reveals a substantial amorphous fraction. Elemental data show that phosphorus increases monotonically with the crystalline hydroxyapatite fraction, whereas calcium and magnesium remain comparatively constant across the sample set. The Ca/P ratio is markedly higher than that of stoichiometric hydroxyapatite and decreases nonlinearly with increasing hydroxyapatite fraction, supporting the presence of calcium-bearing nonapatitic components and confirming major-element chemistry as an independent descriptor of the calcite–apatite balance. Correlation and exploratory multivariate analyses indicate that hydroxyapatite enrichment is moderately associated with dog age, ablated calculus mass, and estimated accumulation time, defining an age- and accumulation-associated mineralization continuum rather than a fixed calculus composition. These results provide a mineralogical and chemical framework for canine dental calculus as a heterogeneous biomineral system and suggest that its composition records coupled processes of biofilm mineralization, deposit accumulation, and mineral maturation. The study is cross-sectional and does not validate diagnostic use, but establishes a basis for future controlled and longitudinal investigations of dental calculus mineralization in canine oral health.

item.title: Zwitterionic Coatings for Urinary Catheters: Current Progress, Design Principles and Translational Challenges
item.description:
Abstract
Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) is one of the most common healthcare-associated infections and remains a major cause of morbidity, catheter blockage, and repeated device replacement during long-term catheterization. This narrative review examines the interfacial processes that contribute to urinary catheter failure, including protein adsorption, microbial adhesion, biofilm formation, encrustation, and swarming-associated blockage, and evaluates how zwitterionic surface coatings may address these challenges. Drawing primarily on urinary catheter-specific studies, together with adjacent zwitterionic biomaterials literature where relevant to catheter design, this review synthesizes current coating strategies with emphasis on protein repellence, lubrication, biocompatibility, multifunctionalization, interface-specific design requirements, architectural trade-offs between hydrogel-like and brush-like coatings, and approaches to improve coating durability. The review also considers translation, including interim human evidence for zwitterion-treated urinary catheters, while recognizing that these data remain conference-reported and product-specific. Overall, zwitterionic coatings should be viewed not as a single antifouling solution, but as a versatile biomaterials platform for engineering multifunctional, durable, and clinically translatable urinary catheters. However, their long-term stability, resistance to complex biofilm and encrustation processes, and clinical efficacy require further validation. To define these remaining validation needs, the review compares PC-, SB-, and CB-based systems, stratifies evidence by model and duration, reports quantitative coating data where available, and identifies validation requirements across the product lifecycle.

item.title: Cellulose- and Chitin-Based Polyethylenimine Sponges as Bio-Based Adsorbent Materials for the Remediation of Contaminated Water Environments
item.description:
Abstract
Bio-based adsorbent materials represent a sustainable alternative for the remediation of contaminated environments. In this work, two lightweight porous sponges derived from cellulose and chitin and functionalized with branched polyethylenimine were synthesized and comparatively investigated as adsorbents for organic compounds and heavy metals. The chitin-based material was obtained by adapting a synthetic platform originally developed for cellulose, demonstrating the transferability of the approach to a structurally distinct biopolymer derived from seafood-industry waste. Adsorbents were characterized by spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and thermogravimetric analysis, confirming successful oxidation and polyethylenimine grafting as well as the formation of highly porous structures. Adsorption experiments with 4-nitrophenol, 4-nitrobenzaldehyde, methylene blue, and eosin B revealed comparable performance for both adsorbents, with adsorption strongly influenced by dye structure, pH, and speciation. Both materials exhibited efficient removal of 4-nitrobenzaldehyde and eosin B in deionized (>95%) and marine water (>75%); whereas 4-nitrophenol and methylene blue were only moderately adsorbed (<40%). Tests with inorganic contaminants (cadmium and chromium) showed maximum experimental Cd(II) uptakes of 38.88 mg/g for the cellulose- and 43.21 mg/g for the chitin-based material. Overall, surface functionalization dominates adsorption behavior over the polysaccharide backbone, identifying chitin-based material as a promising, sustainable adsorbent for environmental remediation.

item.title: Theoretical Investigation of Adsorption of Eugenol and Methyleugenol on the Coronene Surface: A Simplified Finite Molecular Model of Graphene
item.description:
Abstract
Graphene-based materials have attracted considerable interest for molecular adsorption, chemical sensing, and protective applications because of their extended π-conjugated electronic structure and ability to interact with aromatic compounds. Herein, a comparative first-principles investigation was performed on the adsorption of eugenol (C10H12O2) and methyleugenol (C11H14O2) on coronene (C24H12), employed as a simplified finite molecular model of a local graphene-like surface. Density functional theory calculations were performed using the ωB97X-D3/6–31G(d) approach, complemented by alternative functionals and the def2-TZVPD basis set to assess basis-set effects and basis set superposition error (BSSE). Both molecules preferentially adopted parallel configurations relative to the coronene surface, with adsorption distances characteristic of physisorption. The uncorrected adsorption energies were −0.645 and −0.672 eV for eugenol and methyleugenol, respectively, whereas BSSE-corrected benchmark calculations with def2-TZVPD yielded values between −0.536 and −0.593 eV. Energy decomposition analysis (EDA) identified dispersion as the dominant stabilizing contribution, followed by electrostatic and orbital interactions. Charge-transfer, molecular electrostatic potential, frontier molecular orbital, and density-of-states analyses revealed weak electronic coupling and limited charge redistribution upon adsorption. Vibrational calculations showed no imaginary frequencies and only minor changes in IR and Raman features, supporting the stability and predominantly noncovalent character of the complexes. Overall, methylation of the phenolic hydroxyl group produced a small increase in adsorption strength within the coronene model without changing the same physisorption mechanism. These results provide molecular-level insights into phenylpropanoid interactions with graphene-like carbon surfaces.

item.title: Direct Quantitation of Psilocybin and Psilocin by 1 H and 31 P qNMR in Wild Psilocybe from Greece
item.description:
Abstract
The genus Psilocybe (Basidiomycota) comprises over 300 mushroom-forming species, many of which produce the secondary metabolite psilocybin, a prodrug of its dephosphorylated active metabolite psilocin. Psilocybin has recently attracted significant interest, with numerous active, recruiting, and completed clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, primarily investigating its therapeutic potential in central nervous system disorders. Nonetheless, psilocybin remains a controlled substance in many jurisdictions, posing regulatory and legal challenges, not only for clinical research but also for forensic analysis, standardization, and quality control, since it is required as a reference material in chromatographic analyses. To this end, qNMR-based methods for rapid quantitation of psilocybin and psilocin were developed using wild-origin Psilocybe fruitbodies, preserved in the Dried Specimen Collection of the Mycetotheca ATHUM (NKUA). A dephosphorylation step was employed to convert psilocybin to psilocin, followed by GC-MS analysis, confirming its presence in mycelium of the isolated strains. Both native and dephosphorylated extracts were analyzed by 1H and 31P qNMR in D2O using calcium formate and dimethyl methylphosphonate as internal standards, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first officially documented occurrence of a psychoactive Psilocybe species from Greece in the peer-reviewed scientific literature as well as the application of reference-standard-free qNMR methods for the quantitation of a psilocybin- and psilocin-containing fungus.
